title: Rules Hub
bodyHtml:
Below is a collection of Riftbound’s latest rules documents. If you’re ever curious about Riftbounds current rules, regulations, systems and practices, let the below documents be your guide.

Are you wanting to learn Riftbound? Go here instead. The below documents are useful in the way that a car manual is useful when you’re learning to drive. Which is to say, it is useful for some, but probably not yet useful for others.

Constructed Format Legality

Last updated: September 18, 2026

All sets currently produced for Riftbound are legal to be played in sanctioned tournaments at your local game store as well as at larger tournaments. Starting in 2028, we intend to introduce rotation of legal sets for play in Standard Constructed (our primary constructed format.)

2v2 Constructed Legality

Last updated: September 18, 2026

As above, all sets currently produced for Riftbound are legal to be played in sanctioned tournaments.

Core Rules

The Core Rules are the engine that drives a Riftbound game. This document covers deckbuilding rules, timing and resolution of cards and abilities, order of effects, and all the other little rules that define the flow of a game.

Core Rules (last updated: October 9, 2026)

Tournament Rules

The Tournament Rules outline the guidelines for running Riftbound tournaments and deckbuilding guidelines to the Riftbound experience that occur when taking part in an official event.

The Tournament Rules also provide additional guidance for running tournaments and adjudicating issues that arise during play.

Tournament Rules (last updated: October 9, 2026)

Patch Notes

Patch Note articles answer questions and explain the rules and interactions you’ll commonly encounter.

  • Core Rules Patch Notes
  • Spiritforged Patch Notes
  • Unleashed Patch Notes
  • Vendetta Patch Notes
  • Radiance Patch Notes

Errata

With new sets, we issue updates to the rules text on Riftbound cards, called ‘errata.’ Here are the past updates to the rules text for the printed cards.

  • Origins Errata
  • Spiritforged Errata
  • Unleashed Errata
  • Vendetta Errata
  • Radiance Errata

Judges

Are you interested in becoming a Riftbound judge and helping grow the Riftbound community? Judges are one of the backbones of a TCG community helping run events at store and Regional levels.

Take UVS’s judge test and get certified!

title: Vendetta Rules FAQ and Clarifications
bodyHtml:
Welcome to the FAQ for our first worldwide set release, the Vendetta FAQ! These are questions we’ve gathered from public discussion, from judges across the world, and from members of our own team. We appreciate everyone’s excitement and energy as they discussed the rules update for Vendetta; we hope this FAQ will clarify some points that may have been unclear, or provide answers to common questions you may run into.

One point we want to address directly: as we transition to worldwide release, our FAQs have a delicate timing. We want to gather as many real questions from players and judges as possible, while ensuring players aren’t left in the dark for too long on points that are confusing from the new set. If we release the FAQ too early, we might not catch the things that players are finding confusing; while if we release it too late, players can’t use it to prepare themselves and their decks for upcoming events. For future sets, we’re looking to try different models that might reduce some of the pain points players are feeling with this timing, but for now, we appreciate your patience.

The FAQ is a collection of official rulings. In places where the FAQ differs from the Core Rules Document, the FAQ takes precedence. When a new Core Rules Document is released, it will take precedence over any points that differ from this document.

Throughout this document, we use some specific shorthand to represent symbols in card text. Here’s a short guide:

  • [E] means “exhaust”
  • [M] means “Might”
  • [A] means “one power of any domain”
  • [C] means “one power of this card’s domain”
    • [C] in Accelerate costs takes on the domain of the Unit, or turns into [A] if the Unit has no domain or multiple domains.
    • [C] in other cases is treated as the corresponding power symbol in all respects, matching how the cards are actually printed—it’s just a design shorthand!

What happens when you play Abandon on a spell that was played for its Flow cost?

It will be banished when it attempts to leave the chain.

“[T]hen banish it” in flow’s text is short for “if it would leave the chain after becoming a finalized chain item, and leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by its own execution, banish it instead.” Abandon returns the countered card to hand after countering it, but for the purposes of flow’s “then banish it”, this is also leaving the chain. No matter how it happens, as long as the flow spell leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by the execution of the spell itself, it will be banished.

This also applies to effects like Kai’Sa, Evolutionary from Origins, or Fizz, Trickster from Spiritforged.

What is the difference between Iascylla and Azir, Sovereign’s uses of “this battlefield”?

Iascylla’s delayed trigger refers to the battlefield that she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger refers to the battlefield where he is located.

The difference between these two is that Iascylla has a delayed trigger that references implicit information from her trigger condition: the battlefield where she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger does not reference information from his trigger condition, which purely checks for the event of Azir gaining the attacker designation for the first time each combat. Without that information being checked from the trigger condition, the “this battlefield” in Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger will be checked when the triggered ability resolves. If it resolves and he is not located at a battlefield, any instructions related to that battlefield will be ignored; otherwise, the battlefield he is currently located at will be used.

Comparatively, when a triggered ability refers to information from its trigger condition, that information is checked when the ability triggers and not on resolution. In the case of Iascylla, her delayed trigger is linked with her hold effect, so the information from the trigger condition of the hold effect can be shared with the delayed trigger.

In future sets, we’ve moved to use more precise templating and wording for abilities like Iascylla’s.

Relevant Rules: 359.3.f.1., 359.3.f.2., 359.3.f.3., 359.3.f.3.b.

What happens when I play Moonfall choosing an enemy unit while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?

The chosen unit will be given -3 [M]. All other enemy units at the chosen battlefield will be given -2 [M].

Mel, Newly Awakened’s empowered ability is a replacement effect. It replaces the event of a spell or ability you control giving a unit it chooses -[M]. The event it replaces that with is the spell or ability giving an additional -1 [M]. 

Although Moonfall gives -[M] to multiple units, only one of them is chosen, and thus the only event that is eligible to be replaced is the chosen unit being given -2 [M]. It will be replaced with that unit being given -3 [M]. The events of the other units being given -[M] will not be affected by this replacement effect.

Relevant Rules: 370.1., 370.1.b.

What about casting Stupefy while I have an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?

The chosen unit will be given -2 [M], to a minimum of 1 [M]. If it was 2 [M], it will become 1 [M].

In the case of Stupefy, Mel, Newly Awakened replaces the event of Stupefy giving -1 [M] with it giving -2 [M] instead. However, a replacement effect that replaces an event modified by the game effect that generated that event will inherit any of those modifications. In this case, Stupefy modifies the “give -1 [M]” game action and thus event with “to a minimum of 1 [M].” The replaced event will inherit the same modification.

Relevant Rules: 375.

Speaking of Mel, can my opponent play Abandon on my spell while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened? What happens? 

They can play Abandon targeting your spell. On resolution, they will Predict, but nothing else will happen. 

Mel, Newly Awakened says “your spells and abilities can’t be countered.” If the spell can’t be countered, Abandon will attempt to counter it and fail, and then it will replace the event of it being put in the Trash with it being returned to its owner’s hand. However, that event never occurred, so there is nothing for the replacement effect to replace. Thus, Abandon will resolve to no effect. The replacement effect only functions within the limit of the resolution of the ability (it’s not a delayed replacement effect that specifies a duration), so even if the spell resolves later, it will go to the Trash as normal.

How does it work if I cast Abandon while having an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened but they Rebuttal my spell?

In the case of Rebuttal, gaining control of a spell is not the same thing as countering that spell. Effects that prevent spells being countered don’t prevent their controller from changing. If Rebuttal is played choosing your spell, and they pay [A] during resolution of Rebuttal, they will gain control of it. However, them not paying [A] does not mean the spell will be countered.

What new choices can I make when I play Rebuttal and pay [A]?

You can choose any number of targets or modes to make new choices for. The rest remain the same.

If you are remaking choices in this way, any choices you choose not to remake must be legal choices. You can’t choose to have some but not all choices be legal choices. Of course, you can always choose not to make new choices. In that case, any of the current choices will remain in their current state, whether that state is illegal or not.

If a spell has some rules or requirements about the choices made for it, those apply regardless of who controls that spell. For example, if a player plays a spell from face down, they must target game objects located at the battlefield the spell was played from unless the instructions of that spell indicate that a target must be chosen from some other location. Gaining control of such a spell doesn’t change this requirement when making new choices for the spell.

We’ll look at shaping up this section in a future rules update.

What happens if I choose to copy an empowered unit when I equip an unempowered unit with Shady Spectacles?

Being empowered is a status and is not copyable, thus the equipped unit will remain unempowered.

Shady Spectacles applies a copy effect to the equipped unit. Copy effects copy the printed (or copied, if another copy effect has already been applied) traits of the unit being copied. empowered is a status, a temporary modification, and not part of the printed traits of the card, so it will not be copied by Shady Spectacles. Whatever temporary modifications are applied to the unit as the copy effect is executed on that unit will be unaffected by the copy effect. If the unit has Might increases or decreases, a buff, the empowered status, Temporary, attacker, defender, etc those will remain in place.

Relevant Rules: 477.1.b.1.b.

What happens when my opponent’s Akshan, Mischievous steals my equipped Shady Spectacles? What happens if they want to copy Aphelios? 

If it was attached to a unit, the equipped unit loses its copy effect. Akshan will then become a copy of a friendly unit of his controller’s choice. If he becomes a copy of Aphelios, his ability will not trigger.

This question deserves a bit more depth. As of the Vendetta rules update, we have clarified how effects like Shady Spectacles and Svellsongur work; they are replacement effects that replace the event of the equipment being attached to a unit with that event plus whatever their effect specifies. 

In the case of Svellsongur, the resulting series of events will be:

Attach → Copy the equipped unit’s text to Svellsongur’s effect text for as long as Svellsongur is attached

For Shady Spectacles, the resulting series of events will be:

Attach → Choose a friendly unit and make the equipped unit a copy of that unit for as long as Shady Spectacles is attached

These events are not simultaneous. The attach event executes first, and then whatever event is instructed by the replacement effect is executed. Thus, the answer in the Spiritforged FAQ is no longer true: if you attach Svellsongur to Aphelios, he will not trigger twice. Svellsongur doesn’t have the copied effect text when the attach event executes.

Similarly here, if Akshan nabs Shady Spectacles from an opponent, it will attach and then make him a copy. If his controller chooses to make him a copy of Aphelios, it’s too late by that point for his new triggered ability to see the attachment event; it’s already been completed.

Relevant Rules: 369.1., 370.1.b.1., 370.1.a.2.

My Sand Soldier has Shady Spectacles equipped and is a copy of Azir, Ascendent. What happens if I activate the copied Azir’s activatedability before detaching the Shady Spectacles and then attach them to the same Sand Soldier as a copy of the same Azir, Ascendent? Can I use the activated ability again?

You can.

Each instance of the copied ability is a different ability. The game object remains the same throughout this whole process, so any temporary modifications will remain on the Sand Soldier as it transforms, but the copied rules text is an entirely new instance of the ability. It is the same idea as Svellsongur’s copy of an ability being “refreshed” if Svellsongur is detached and then reattached to the same unit.

What happens during combat damage assignment if my 4 [M] unit has both Ki Barrier and Lotus Trap played on it this turn and my opponent has a 4 [M] defender?

You can order the replacement effects on your unit. If Ki Barrier is first, your unit will take no damage and you will have 3 damage prevention remaining on your unit. If Lotus Trap is first, your unit will take 1 damage and will have no damage prevention remaining on your unit.

With the Vendetta rules update, we’ve streamlined how replacement effects that apply to damage work in combat. Specifically, any replacement effect that would apply to combat damage being dealt will apply instead to combat damage assignment. This was already the case for prevention effects like Ki Barrier or Counterstrike, to prevent several strange edge cases. Now, damage increasing replacement effects will also apply during damage assignment. 

Relevant Rules: 465.2.c.4.a., 465.2.c.5.

What happens when I discard a Patched Porobot with Hwei, Brooding Painter’s move trigger?

Two triggers will go on the chain, in the order of your choosing. One says “Give me +3 [M] this turn.” while the other says “Ready up to 2 runes.”

Hwei, Brooding Painter says “do the following based on the discarded card's type …” Unlike our previous reflexive triggers printed on cards that use a similar template (cf Twisted Fate, Gambler), Hwei doesn’t say “do one of the following …” As long as the card has the appropriate type, you will put the corresponding reflexive trigger on the chain. If somehow there existed a card that was a spell unit gear, you would put three reflexive triggers on the chain when you discard it to Hwei.

Relevant Rules: 387.1.b.

If my opponent plays two spells in succession, can I counter the first one with Crumbling Sands?

Yes.

Crumbling Sands uses the “finalize” meaning of play, because it checks whether cards have been “played” and isn’t a triggered ability. As long as an opponent (not even necessarily the one who played this spell) has chosen targets, paid costs, checked legality, and completed the process of finalizing another spell, even if that spell was countered, Crumbling Sands can counter a spell. That means it can counter the first spell played, as long as another spell was played by an opponent after that one.

Relevant Rules: 419.4.b.

When can I react to my opponent playing Fallen Feline to a battlefield? And how does naming a card work?

You can react to the play effect of Fallen Feline, before they’ve named a spell.

Fallen Feline’s play effect instructs its controller to name a spell. This occurs on resolution of the triggered ability. If Fallen Feline is played to a battlefield, as soon as the ability resolves, opponents cannot play spells with that name. Meaning spells by that name can not be put onto a chain. Any spells already on the chain when Fallen Feline’s ability resolves will be unaffected. However, by the time you know the chosen spell it’s too late to play that spell.

Naming a card or tag has new rules with the Vendetta rules update. When naming something in this way, the overarching rule that applies to all naming is that you can’t name something that doesn’t exist in Riftbound. You can’t name the “Locke” tag, the “totem” type, nor a card named “Lingering Tentacles,” because none of those has been printed on cards or tokens in Riftbound.

However, you can name a card using information that uniquely identifies it. That information could be its name, but it could just as well be something like “the [3] spell with Flow that makes tentacles” or “the red Kai’Sa” or “Illaoi.” As long as there is no ambiguity as to what card is being named, a player can use whatever method is clear to their opponents and teammates. You can’t name a card by saying just “Kai’Sa” if there are two or more cards that could be identified in that way—you won’t have named a card if that’s all you say.

Relevant Rules: 761., 761.1., 761.2., 762., 762.1., 762.2.

If I disempower a Kayle, Justified who has been empowered 3 times, does she lose all of her empowered statuses?

No. She will lose one of her empowered statuses.

For every Riftbound card other than Kayle, empowered is a binary status. They are either empowered or not. Kayle utilizes the golden rule “Card text supersedes rules text” to overcome this and be able to escape the normal bounds of what the empowered status means. On Kayle, empowered isn’t a binary status but a stacking status; she can have up to 3 empowered statuses. When Kayle is disempowered, the disempower action attempts to remove the empowered status. If she only has one empowered status, great, it’s gone. If she has more than one empowered status, the disempower action will remove one of the empowered statuses from Kayle.

But can I activate Kayle’s empower ability even if she’s already empowered?

Yes.

Kayle’s empower ability can be activated any number of times. If she has less than 3 empowered statuses, she will become empowered. If she has 3 empowered statuses, the ability can still be activated but nothing will happen when the ability resolves.

What happens if my opponent plays Flash on their Akali, Silent that’s currently in combat after I play Star-Crossed targeting her?

Akali will be unaffected by Star Crossed as it resolves.

Akali, Silent is what the rules refer to as “untargetable” for enemy spells and abilities when she isn’t in combat; meaning she is not a legal target for them. Enemy spells and abilities being played when she’s untargetable can’t choose her. If she becomes untargetable after she’s already been chosen by an effect and retains it as that effect begins to resolve, it will “mistarget” her. She will be unaffected by any of the spell or ability’s instructions. If an instruction chooses only her, that instruction will be ignored.

Relevant Rules: 757.1., 758., 758.1.

I have a Ravenbloom Student on the board and I haven’t played any spells this turn. What happens when I play Rebuttal targeting my opponent’s Stupefy and pay [A] on resolution? After everything resolves, how much will Battering Ram cost? Will my opponent’s Legion abilities be active?

Ravenbloom Student will trigger twice, Battering Ram will cost [4], and your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active.

Ravenbloom Student’s triggered ability checks whether a spell that you control resolves. You gained control of the Stupefy, and it resolved, so you will have triggered Ravenbloom Student’s ability. Battering Ram and Legion, on the other hand, check whether cards were finalized. Although you gained control of Stupefy, you did not finalize it; you got it after it was already finalized by your opponent. Thus, your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active, and Battering Ram will only receive a [1] Energy discount.

Relevant Rules: 419.4., 419.4.a., 419.4.b.

What happens when I conquer with Swain, Visionary, if I’ve only played a Patched Porobot and Stupefy this turn?

You will score 2 points total. 1 from conquering, 1 from Swain.

Swain only checks whether you’ve played a non-token unit, a non-token gear, and a spell. Checks like that do not care whether they were satisfied by multiple cards or a single card relevant to the trigger conditions.

What happens when my opponent plays Switcheroo on their 2 [M] unit and my empowered Gangplank, Naval?

Gangplank, Naval will replace his Might being lowered with him being given +3 [M] this turn.

Swap calculates the difference in Might and generates two effects: an increase, and a decrease. When a swap effect is applied to two units’ Mights, it gives those units +[M] and -[M] respective to who has the higher Might. 

Under the hood, Gangplank’s replacement effect sees the event of him being given -[M] and replaces it with him being given +3 [M] this turn instead. The event of the other unit being given +[M] is unaffected by Gangplank’s replacement effect. By the time we apply the replacement effect, the difference between the two units has been calculated. In the example with the 2 [M] unit, the final Mights of the two units will be 2 [M] → 6 [M], and 6 [M] → 9 [M].

The way this works is not immediately obvious based on how the swap game action rules are written. We will clarify this in a future rules update. 

Note that this logic also applies to Mel, Newly Awakened and Switcheroo.

What happens when my empowered Gangplank, Naval is moved by my opponent’s Blast Cone’s play effect and they exhaust Blast Cone to stun Gangplank? Will he be stunned? What happens if I then play Back Off choosing my Gangplank? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?

Blast Cone will stun Gangplank. If you play Back Off choosing your stunned Gangplank, he will not receive +3 [M] this turn.

Blast Cone’s triggered ability that stuns units doesn’t choose them, so Gangplank’s replacement effect can’t apply to that event. Back Off played on a stunned Gangplank does not actually perform the stun game action, because Gangplank is already stunned. It’s legal to play Back Off, but the instruction will be negated. In order for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace an event of him being stunned, the stun game action must actually be performed. Similarly, if an effect that said “Friendly units can’t be stunned” were active with a friendly empowered Gangplank, Naval is on the board, a stun effect that is played choosing Gangplank wouldn’t generate an event that Gangplank could replace, because no stun game action is performed.

Relevant Rules: 423.1.a.1.

What happens if I play Stupefy on my 1 [M] empowered Gangplank, Naval? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?

He will not.

In order for his replacement effect to apply, the event of him being given -[M] must occur. In the case of Stupefy played on a 1 [M] unit, no -[M] is given; it is snapshot to -0 [M]. Thus, there is no suitable event for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace.

Relevant Rules: 477.3.b.

What happens when my opponent plays Hidden Blade targeting my Akali, Deadly Weapon in reaction to her move trigger? Will it still deal damage to the chosen unit?

It will.

Akali is another case where her ability refers to information implicit to its own trigger condition, similar to Iascylla. Akali’s “battlefield I moved to or from” doesn’t require her to be on the board in order for us to be able to identify it, nor does it reference information about her current state. Even if she leaves the board, that information was checked when her ability triggered, and it is still available to us on resolution.

Relevant Rules: 359.3.f.3.

Can I activate an empowered Heimerdinger, Inventor to ready 2 gear if my Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow legend isn’t empowered? What about if my Heimerdinger isn’t empowered?

You can activate Heimerdinger’s ability if he is empowered, regardless of the empowered status of Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow.

There is a bit of a trick here, in that there are two important details to this question relating to dependent keywords:

  1. First is that a dependent keyword (the kind of ability that [Level][>] or [Empowered][>] are when they appear with the arrow) includes the whole of the ability, including the dependent ability. They’re all one object, so to speak. 
  2. Second is that a dependent keyword’s dependent ability still exists and can be referenced while it is inactive—that is, if its condition isn’t met. In this case, the condition is that the source of the ability is empowered.

Heimerdinger gains all activated abilities that have the [E] symbol in their cost, and he gains the entire ability, restrictions, costs, dependent keywords and all. In effect, Defender of Tomorrow’s ability that Heimerdinger is gaining is the whole line that says:

[Empowered][>] [1], [E]: Ready 2 gear.

Heimerdinger can gain this ability even if Defender of Tomorrow isn’t empowered because of that second point we made previously.

The key rule for this case is 727.1.b.1., which reads:

The Dependent Ability is present on the card for the sake of reference or evaluation until the Condition is met.

This means that the ability isn’t active and its text isn’t being processed yet, but other effects can reference or evaluate its text before the condition is met. Heimerdinger, Inventor is exactly one such effect.

Relevant Rules: 727.1., 727.1.b., 727.1.b.1.

What card does Astral Heron’s triggered ability discount?

It discounts the next card played (added to the chain and queued for finalization) this turn after the ability resolves.

Astral Heron has received an erratum to update its wording: “When you play your first card each turn, if I'm at a battlefield, the next card you play this turn costs [2][A][A] less.”

What happens when I play Temporal Breach targeting my Elder Dragon in base and pay [A][A] for Dragon Roost while playing Elder Dragon? Will it be played to base or to Dragon Roost?

You can choose which of those two locations you want to play it to.

In general, there are not many cases where we have this kind of competing instruction: one effect that tells you to play a unit to one location, and one that tells you to play it to another. That being said, when they do arise with contradictory requirements, the precedent from other areas of the rules is that the player chooses one of those requirements and ignores all others.

Note that this only applies to mandatory positive requirements, ones that specify a location or method without also preventing the action from being performed to other locations or with other methods and that aren’t optional. For example, an effect like Perched Grimwyrm’s passive ability is a restriction on playing that unit to any location other than a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Rockfall Path’s passive ability is a restriction on playing units to Rockfall Path. If you’ve conquered only Rockfall Path this turn, you can’t play Perched Grimwyrm at all, because those two restrictions are contradictory.

In this case, the contradictory requirements don’t directly prohibit the playing of these units to other locations, so we can choose one of the contradictory requirements and ignore the rest.

What happens when I play Perched Grimwyrm while I haven’t conquered Dragon Roost this turn? Can I pay [A][A] and play it to Dragon Roost? What if I’ve conquered another battlefield this turn?

You cannot.

In Riftbound, “can’t” beats “can.” Perched Grimwyrm’s effect is a “can’t,” as in it can’t be played to any location but to a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Dragon Roost’s ability tries to give the Grimwyrm permission to be played to the Roost, but that can’t overcome Perched Grimwyrm’s own restriction. If you have no ability to play Perched Grimwyrm to Dragon Roost after paying for it, you will not be able to finalize Perched Grimwyrm at all. The actions taken as part of playing Perched Grimwyrm will be undone and it will be returned to the zone it was played from.

This is true even if you’ve conquered another battlefield this turn. If you have the ability, you can play Perched Grimwyrm to that battlefield without paying the additional cost of Dragon Roost, but you can’t play it to Dragon Roost itself unless you’ve conquered it.

Sharp eyed readers may remember that Baron Nashor doesn’t work this way. He enters at the Baron Pit regardless of effects preventing him from being played to battlefields. The reason for this is that Baron Nashor’s passive ability generates a delayed replacement effect, the one that reads “I enter there.” This replacement effect replaces the event of him entering to any other location with him entering to the Baron Pit. The replacement effect gets around effects like Mageseeker Warden which limit where you can play units. However, Dragon Roost is not written as a replacement effect. It tells you where to play the dragon you’ve paid the additional cost for, but it doesn’t specify how that dragon enters the board. Therefore it is a permission on play location, but not a replacement effect.

Relevant Rules: 054.2., 369.3.

Can I disempower my Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer to empower my Kayle? Do I control my own legend?

Yes, you can disempower Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer. And yes, you control your own legend.

We don’t typically consider the possibility that any player controls a legend, because control of legends cannot change, but you do indeed control your own legend.

What happens if I play Dragon Form on a unit that has -1 [M] from Stupefy applied to it? Will my Fiora, Grand Duelist trigger? Is there a moment where my unit becomes 5 [M] before the -1 [M] from Stupefy brings it down to 4 [M]?

She will not trigger.

Although Dragon Form sets the base Might of a unit to 5 [M], it does so via layers. Layers are evaluated when the effect is applied and their evaluation includes all existing applied layer alterations. We process layers in order, starting from the Trait-Altering layer (where this base Might setting effect is applied), proceeding to the Ability-Altering layer (not part of this example), and proceeding to the Arithmetic layer (where Stupefy’s -1 [M] is applied), but this process happens instantaneously; there is no window while evaluating layers for the unit to see itself become 5 [M] and then go down to 4 [M]. As soon as the effect of Dragon Form is applied, the unit is 4 [M].

As a side note, Might is one of the traits that is managed in the Trait-Altering layer, and it is one of the copyable traits that copy effects can replace or add to.

What happens when I play Hostile Takeover gaining control of my opponent’s ready unit, move it to base, and then play Temporal Breach choosing it? Where will the unit go?

The unit will remain in Banishment.

Units cannot be played to a base of a player other than their own controller under any circumstances. Because the owner of the unit is the one being instructed to play the unit, and the location they are being instructed to play it to is a base other than their own, it isn’t possible to play the unit. During the check legality step of finalization, the unit will be returned to banishment from the chain and all actions taken will be undone.

My 11 Might Renekton, Brute is disempowered by my own Profiteer. What happens when my opponent plays Stupefy choosing him? Will his ability trigger? What happens if instead I activated his ability?

Renekton’s ability will not trigger in either scenario.

In order to “become 10 or more,” his Might would have to have previously been less than 10. “10 or more” is a state, and Renekton’s triggered ability checks for the event of him achieving that state. If he maintains that state, regardless of how his Might changes, he will not “become” that state.

What happens when I play Icathian Rain choosing a Recruit at Heisho, Shell of the World once and Irelia, Fervent in base five times? How many times do I pay for deflect?

You will not pay for deflect.

While your spell or ability chooses a unit at Heisho, Shell of the World, you ignore deflect while paying for the spell. Ignore, in this context, means you treat deflect on the specified units as being inactive, like it’s turned off temporarily. In the case of Heisho, it doesn’t specify any units whose deflect to ignore, so you ignore all instances of deflect on units.

This only applies to the specified spell or ability. You can’t play a spell or ability choosing a unit at Heisho, and then play another one choosing a unit at another location and not at Heisho and still ignore deflect. Only while at least one target of the spell or ability is a unit located at Heisho do you ignore deflect while paying costs for that spell or ability.

Relevant Rules: 766., 767.

What happens when I play Hextech Ray on an Elder Dragon while Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger is active and I have an Immortal Phoenix in the Trash? Can I play Immortal Phoenix from the Trash?

You can.

Per the current rules, there is nothing that would stop Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger from triggering Immortal Phoenix. It is a triggered ability generated by a spell; it is attributed a kill action, and thus the spell that generated it will also be attributed the same kill action. The owner of Imperial Decree is the controller of the delayed triggered ability; the player responsible for the kill action is the one who controls the ability; and that same player is the owner of Immortal Phoenix in the Trash. Thus all three conditions for Immortal Phoenix triggering are complete, and it will trigger.

If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens?

They will be readied.

This is a rules quirk that players and judges identified as a result of a small additional rule added in the Vendetta rules update. We’re going to give some clarity to this that will resolve this issue, but if you don’t understand the conversation or why it is necessary, don’t worry. This isn’t an actual change to how we’ve been interpreting and ruling cards, but smoothing out a bug.

In short, the linked instructions rules are too expansive currently on what qualifies as an “ignored” instruction. To clarify this definition: an ignored instruction is one that wasn’t performed as part of the execution of a spell or ability’s instructions because it mistargeted (i.e. because the targeted object wasn’t a legal target on resolution). This is a case where, for example, you play Hidden Blade choosing an enemy unit and they play Star-Crossed in reaction, returning their unit to hand. When Hidden Blade resolves, the unit isn’t on the board, so we ignore the “Its controller draws 2.” instruction. Alternatively, if Hidden Blade is given the Repeat keyword by the Academy and both executions target the same unit, this is the reason why the unit’s controller doesn’t draw 4 cards.

An instruction is not ignored if an ability, effect, or circumstance of the game prevents it from occurring. This could take the form of a replacement effect that replaces the event of the instruction with something else, it could take the form of an ability like Vilemaw’s Lair that says “Units can’t move from here to base.” or it could take the form of a game action like Buff or Ready being performed on a unit that already has the appropriate state. It could even take the form of a unit, gear, or spell no longer being in an appropriate zone as long as the instruction doesn’t target those objects. The instruction in these cases isn’t ignored, but instead negated. A negated instruction has its effects skipped, replaced, or prevented. A negated instruction will not cause any linked instructions to be ignored unless those instructions refer specifically to the action being performed.

Some examples:

  1. If a unit at a battlefield says “I can’t be killed.” and a player plays Hidden Blade choosing that unit, the unit’s controller will still draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The instruction was negated and not ignored, so the linked instruction will still execute.)
  2. If a unit at a battlefield is chosen by Hidden Blade and in reaction its controller plays Flash moving it to base, that unit’s controller will not draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The instruction was ignored, so any linked instructions will be ignored.)
  3. If a unit at a battlefield is chosen by Hidden Blade and in reaction its controller plays Zhonya’s Hourglass, that unit’s controller will draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The unit is on the board and can have its information checked, and the instruction was negated and not ignored.)
  4. If a unit at a battlefield has been affected by Smite previously this turn and it is chosen by Hidden Blade, that unit’s controller will not draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (Although the instruction is executed, the unit is not on the board to have its information checked. Additionally, the unit was moved to a non-board zone by an effect other than Hidden Blade and thus no longer has a controller that Hidden Blade can reference.)

title: October 2026 Tournament Rules Changelog
bodyHtml:
Hey Riftbounders,

Vriss here with a new Tournament Rules Update! Today’s rules go into effect with the Radiance Pre-Rift on October 16, 2026.

While this update may look large, it mostly involves cleaning up small mistakes and adding clarity for judges where it was lacking. I’d like to give a huge shoutout to the Riftbound judge community for all the amazing feedback that helped inform this update, especially @benediktwerner for collating a ton of information and sending it our way. Riftbound thrives when we can work with players and judges to provide the best Organized Play experience possible.

For a detailed breakdown of all the changes, see the bulleted list below. For a link to the full Tournament Rules document, look here:

[Tournament rules doc link]

While we’ve come a long way developing and improving the Tournament Rules, we see a need to share more about our philosophy and thought processes behind this document. We’re working on a new companion document for the Tournament Rules which fully breaks down the philosophy and intent behind each rule, especially for the judge perspective. More details to come soon!

Changing Gameplay Decisions

Before letting you dive into the nitty gritty, I want to elaborate on Riftbound’s Gameplay Decision policy (509. in the Tournament Rules).

The Gameplay Decisions policy exists to give players some flexibility when making decisions (we are not aiming for an equivalent of chess’ touch-move), but it is not meant to allow players to take back errors once their opponent is required to call information to their attention. 

For example:

  • Player A moves their 3 Might unit to a battlefield and passes focus. 
  • Player B indicates their 2 Might unit at that battlefield is now at 4 Might due to their legend, Wuju Bladesman. 
  • Player A can no longer change their decision to move to that battlefield and pass focus.

High Organized Play Level (OPL) Riftbound events have the highest level of competitive integrity, valuing player’s skills and abilities to evaluate the game and make strategically correct tactical decisions. At high OPL, we never want it to feel like you need to play the game for your opponent or get punished for your opponent’s mistakes.

(At casual OPL, allowing an opponent to take back a mistake like this is not required, but it is encouraged for sportsmanship and learning.)

Changelog

  • Increased clarity on when players can change gameplay decisions.
    • Updated 509.5. - 509.6.b., renumbered following.
  • Completely reworked Deck Presentation Error remedies to be clearer and better describe their intent, and detail missing Chosen Champions remedies for all OPLs.
    • Updated 703.4.b. and its sub-bullets.
  • Clarified that loops must be fully deterministic and include no random elements. Added examples.
    • Added 505.2. - 505.2.b. and 505.13.
  • Clarified that knowingly attempting to engage in Improperly Determining a Winner is cheating, increased penalty at Professional OPL.
    • Added 703.10.d. - 703.10.e.
  • Further defined Floor Judge responsibility on correcting errors they see, even if they are not called by a player.
    • Added 204.5.c. - 204.5.c.1., renumbered following
  • Added clarity to when penalties should be upgraded based on being advantageous to the erroring player.
    • Added 702.1.d. - 702.1.d.1.
  • Added Radiance to Standard sets.
    • Added 601.3.c.6. - 601.3.c.6.a.
  • Expanded Facedown Card Error to include when cards illegally leave a facedown zone.
    • Rewrote 702.13. and its sub-bullets.
  • Added Might/Might Bonus to the parts of a card that must remain intact when a card is altered.
    • Updated 419.4.a.
  • Clarified that players are allowed to bluff about their private information.
    • Added 502.11. and renumbered following.
  • Clarified that tokens must be represented by card objects with a clear ready state and must be understandable by opponents when used.
    • Updated 508.8.
  • Clarified “choosing” things, lethal damage, and adding resources as examples of observable impact for triggers.
    • Added 506.3.e.10. - 506.3.e.12.
  • Added a requirement for the state of additional turns to be communicated between players.
    • Added 502.4.b. and renumbered following,
  • Clarified that when applying remedies, a “full round cycle” completes when the player whose turn the error occurred on begins their next turn.
    • Added 702.1.e.
  • Added missing penalties for illegally scouting matches or using electronic devices at inappropriate times.
    • Updated 410.4. and added 703.9.g.
  • Clarified that randomized deck checks should occur at the start of a round and should verify all deck elements, added some process clarification.
    • Added 411.3.a. Updated 411.3. and renumbered following
  • Corrected typo in Mispayment for Cost remedy.
    • Updated 702.9.b.3.
  • Fixed missing/incorrect number references.
    • Added 602.1.a.3. Updated 406.1.d. , 702.2.b.
  • Clarified that Battlefields can’t be reused if a game loss is applied after Battlefields have been revealed.
    • Added 406.1.c. and renumbered following.
  • Changed the Overpayment for Cost remedies to not include giving the erroring player floating resources if a simple rewind is not possible.
    • Updated 702.8.b.1.
  • Clarified that players may look at outside notes during sideboarding and after Battlefields are revealed, but must stop once opening hands are drawn (before mulligans).
    • Updated 416.4. - 416.5
  • Clarified that best-of-one sideboarding does not apply to limited competitions.

  • Clarified Failure to Maintain Game State warnings are fully exempt from upgrades.

title: Riftbound Core Rules: Patch Notes
bodyHtml:
Welcome to Riftbound’s first official Rules Update Patch! This will be a big one—not necessarily because of the volume of changes or shifts in how players playing already are going to be interacting with the game, but because it is the first time we are changing our Official Rules Documents (ORD)! This patch is specifically updating the Core Rules (CR) and not the Tournament Rules (TR), and the following changes will go over the broad areas of interest in more detail.

These notes are not comprehensive or exhaustive, but meant to draw attention to the most broad areas of focus so we have a stage to discuss intent and clarify the point of the largest and most sweeping changes in the document. If we had a line item for every comma and other punctuation change, this article would begin to rival some sections of the rules themselves.

Before diving in: It may seem odd for us to be delivering changes to a card game as “Patch Notes.” We get it. However we wanted to keep you, our players, informed and up to date on our intentions and thinking about the game. Given that we already do things a little differently, and a patch note format is something we have experience writing, why not format things this way?

Origins has already had the initial rules release, the FAQ, and now this update. That’s because it’s the first set and we’re still getting our rules situated. We anticipate a more regular rules update cadence in the future.

You may have already seen the [FAQ] we posted a few weeks ago. A lot of that information is repeated in these notes, as the Core Rules now reflect the rules that inform those answers. A very small amount of that information is explicitly contradicted in these notes and in the new rules, as our continuing work on the rules led us to different conclusions. We’ll point it out explicitly when that’s the case.

Contents of this Patch

As previously mentioned,  these notes are not a comprehensive changelog, but instead the grouping of major points of change to the rules players should be aware of.

Many rules have changed their number as a result of this. Some rules are new, and are numbered for the first time. Some entire sections may have moved. For the most part, changes of this nature are not mentioned here.

The rules updates and clarifications from our recent [FAQ] are present and iterated in these notes, such as the addition of pending chain items, triggered abilities evaluating their conditions based on the destination of the triggering game object, the implications of individual card errata, and more.

However there are also new clarifications and changes that were not mentioned in the FAQ that are important to go over! Those are detailed below. These changes have been detailed to the community directly in some cases. In other cases they are rules interactions and cases we caught ourselves and wanted to make crystal clear. 

Patch Notes

New Silver Rules

Our Silver Rules are where we want to express broad rules and concepts across the game that are nearly always true. Considering cards often supersede them, and exceptions are very common, Silver Rules are where we keep the concepts that have vanishingly few exceptions. Not zero, but few. We have two more to add because of how often we found ourselves repeating them.

  • NEW RULE: Can’t beats can.
  • NEW RULE: “Do as much as you can”, otherwise known as DAMAYC.

Adjustments to Foundational Definitions

We have some housekeeping to get out of the way, mostly consisting of us clarifying existing rules and making sure implied rules were written out explicitly. 

  • Clarified: You cannot ready something that is already ready. It can be targeted with an effect that will ready it, but it will not become ready for the sake of triggers or other game effects. This was already spelled out for exhaust, so ready should match.
  • Clarified: Domain Identity is keyed off of Champion Legend.
  • Clarified: Corrected vague language in the rules regarding Domain.
  • Clarified: A player’s Chosen Champion is not one specific piece of cardboard, but any Champion Unit with the same name as the Chosen Champion that began the game in the Champion Zone.
  • Clarified: The Champion Zone has a maximum occupancy of 1.
  • Clarified: The Main Deck is secret information.
    • It is a secret to everyone.
  • Clarified: When cards are returned to players’ hands, they are returned to their owners’ hands only. 
    • You might be friends enough to share, but that isn’t a game mechanic.
  • Clarified: When cards are recycled, they are only recycled by their owner, regardless of which player is instructed to recycle them.

Minor Deckbuilding Clarification

  • Clarified: Players cannot have duplicate battlefields among their 3 battlefields.
  • New Rule: In 2v2, partners cannot include the same battlefield across both of their decks.

This is something many players intuited, but it wasn’t made directly clear. We want battlefields to be a source of variance and expression, and that is undermined if both players bring the same battlefield—worse if they each bring three of the same battlefield. We played it this way internally and simply overlooked its definition in the rules. So it is now clear and outlined as intent.

Speaking of 2v2 rules…

2v2 Adjustments

There are a few clarifications and new rules for 2v2. We want players on teams to act as one unit, and to that end we want them to consider things in a combined and intentional way when approaching this way of playing.

  • NEW RULE: Allied players cannot repeat battlefields in their decks.
    • Already said this, but it bore repeating
  • NEW RULE: Players cannot have the same Champion Legend as their partner.
    • This was how we tested and played internally, and is a key thought behind the intent of how players approach this format.
  • CLARIFIED: Partners win or lose together. This means one player conceding has their partner lose as well.
  • Rule 650: No change
  • Card Details
    • CLARIFIED: Cards with subtitles have the subtitles as part of their name.
    • CLARIFIED: References to cards’ costs always mean their base cost.
    • NEW RULE: Defined Tags, Domains, Types, and Supertypes.
    • CLARIFIED: More clearly defined details about shorthands for Exhaust and Might.
    • CLARIFIED: Clearly defined shorthand for Domains.

We made a bunch of definitions more easy to find, and less needed to intuit. Now it is easy to follow along with the way we write out cards in plaintext without needing to know the arcane secrets of letters and brackets. We just let everyone in on the Card Cant.

Damage, Deal, and Heal

  • NEW RULE: Damage is now defined.
    • It is really weird we didn’t do this before. Seems like we all might be a little bit game-rotted.
  • NEW RULE: Deal is now defined as a game action.
  • NEW RULE: Heal is now defined as a game action.
    • Also weird that these weren’t defined, but now they are!

Bonus Damage

  • CLARIFIED: Bonus Damage is now properly defined.
  • CLARIFIED: More clearly defined how Bonus Damage interacts with the Deal action.

Bonus Damage for the most part was an easily understood fantasy. If Void Seeker normally deals 4 damage and is dealing 1 Bonus Damage, now it deals 5. However we needed more explicit and detailed rules about how it should interact with our more complex spells and abilities, and the rules were vague in those sections. So we clarified the intent here.

Removal of Relevant Players and the Invite Mechanic in FFA 

Please put down the torches and pitchforks. We get to the first intentionally functional change and it is one that will be divisive but bear with us. This was not an easy decision for us, as every time we explained the “Relevant Player” system for Free-For-All, players’ eyes would light up with the potential. The idea of being invited to betray their friends, or the decisions for table politics—they obviously felt all that was exciting and interesting, and we agree!

However, in practice these rules instead created situations where players were powerless to defend themselves in FFA games, and that is a worse situation. We are removing the system wholesale because, as we are fond of saying, the juice is not worth the squeeze. 

  • REMOVAL: Concept of “Relevant Players” has been stricken from the Core Rules.
  • CLARIFIED: All players always have agency to act during Showdowns and Chains in all modes.

Basic Rune Abilities

  • CLARIFIED: Basic rune abilities have Reaction.
    • They always did.
    • We forgot.

Pending and Finalizing

This is a topic we discussed in our recent FAQ, but now we have the full rules available for perusal. The process is detailed as well as the result. The process has its own acronym, FEPR, and the outcome, pending and finalizing, has helped us sequence and control our unique method of card effects and sequencing consistently.

One thing to note is that there is one functional change amidst this new system that has a notable impact on players already familiar with the existing rules: Players can now refuse Deflect costs incurred by triggered abilities. This will result in the triggered ability failing to finalize on the chain. 

  • NEW SYSTEM: Pending and finalizing have been added and detailed. For a more detailed explanation, please see the [FAQ].
  • NEW SYSTEM: FEPR: Finalize, Execute, Pass, Resolve. This is the process through which chains are resolved and has been detailed.
    • Felicia Fifer FEPR’d a Flute of Fixin’s
  • NEW RULE: Triggered abilities that incur a cost when put on the chain may be refused. This will cause them to fail to be finalized.

Reflexive Triggers

Reflexive triggers are now clearly communicated. These were also discussed in our recent [FAQ]. Notable is that we have clarified when triggered abilities from spells are still part of the spell—and when they are not.

  • NEW RULE: Defined reflexive triggers and how to identify them.
  • NEW RULE: Defined how reflexive triggers interact with Bonus Damage.
  • CLARIFIED: Made more clear that triggered abilities originating from spells are part of the spell for considerations of kill attribution, but are still abilities for the sake of effects such as “Counter a spell.”

Numbering sections

Many sections have had numbers appended to the text of their rules to clarify that they are sequentially processed:

  • Steps of playing a card
  • Cleanups
  • Layers
  • Steps of combat

The Steps of Combat

  • CLARIFIED: Initial Chain population sequence (Attacker, Everyone Else, Defender)
  • CLARIFIED: Focus does not pass at the end of the initial chain.
    • This is so that who gets to play first in a showdown is not reliant on whether or not there was an initial chain.
  • CLARIFIED: Defined more clearly when and how the Attacker and Defender designations are gained.
  • CLARIFIED: Spelled out the end of combat sequence.
  • CLARIFIED: Assigning and dealing combat damage are now clearly and separately defined.
  • CLARIFIED: Combat Cleanup defined as a Special Cleanup.

The steps of combat needed some attention for clarity. The sequence of how things started and ended were just vague enough to cause some confusion, and with this, and some work mentioned later to clarify around the contested status, we believe this will make the systems easier to follow for the more rules-ingrained among our players.

What’s a “Special Cleanup,” you ask? An excellent segue to the next section…

Cleanups

  • CLARIFIED: Made the cleanup step as a whole much more robust—when they occur, what happens during them (and what doesn’t), and what order those things happen in.
    • They now happen all the time. Figuratively.
  • NEW RULE: Cleanups occur repeatedly until a cleanup occurs with nothing of note occurring.
  • NEW RULE: Introduced the concept of Special Cleanups. A Special Cleanup has unique steps inserted, and if it repeats, a normal cleanup is what repeats until nothing of note occurs.

We wanted our cleanup step to do a lot of things. Some of those things only need to happen under very specific circumstances, but others needed to happen repeatedly, almost constantly. Rather than create situations with awkward reminders or exceptions, we created the Special Cleanups with a simpler rule of thumb for players to remember: Cleanups repeat, and Special Cleanups happen once. If a Special Cleanup needs to repeat, it repeats into a normal cleanup.

Contested Status and Control

  • CLARIFIED: Made more clear the process of contesting battlefields.
    • Related to Attacker and Defender designations.
  • NEW RULE: Players now can’t lose control of battlefields while a battlefield is contested, even if they have no units there.
  • CLARIFIED: Spelled out how control is established, and when specifically the contested status is removed from battlefields.
  • CLARIFIED: Made clear that if a player moves units into a battlefield that a differing player had moved to, and opened a showdown for, the current showdown will end and a second showdown will begin alongside combat beginning.
    • We call this “surprise defense.”
  • CLARIFIED: Control of a battlefield establishes control of its abilities.
  • NEW RULE: Defined the concept of neutral abilities and how to handle them.
  • CLARIFIED: Made it clear that control is established at the end of a non-combat showdown.

The concept of contested status is a key part of the state machine that keeps control and conquering flowing in our game. This helps make clear the logic of that machinery. We also defined a few interactions that we answered directly to the community but that weren’t entirely written in black-and-white in the CR—namely the concept of “surprise defense” and “conquering on defense,” both of which are now well documented in the rules.

Showdowns and Combat Staging

  • EDIT: Combat is now “staged” instead of “pending.”
  • CLARIFIED: Showdowns are now marked as staged.

This is a lexicon change to ensure ongoing clarity. Pending means more for the pending and finalize systems, so combat and showdowns are Staged going forward. Showdowns weren’t previously marked as pending but were handled similarly to pending combats, so we brought them along in the new terminology.

Targeting and Choosing

  • CLARIFIED: Targeting has clear definitions.
  • CLARIFIED: “Valid target” has a rote definition.
  • NEW RULE: Move destinations are a required choice. This means they are required to be made at time of putting a spell or ability on the chain. It also means that you cannot choose destinations that are not valid to satisfy the conditions of a spell or ability. 

Targeting in our game is complex. This is partially because we have so many moving parts and partially because we have opted to write our cards in a way that nine times out of ten are in plain conversational language. However, this means that getting to the nitty gritty interpretation can get hairy sometimes. We can’t put a Riftbound designer in every game store to answer your targeting questions, so now the rules answer them instead.

Null Isn’t Zero 

  • CLARIFIED: Clarified that unavailable numerical information always resolves to a null value rather than to 0.

This is an odd sentiment, but it can be easily understood with Baited Hook. If you target a unit with Baited Hook, and before the effect resolves that unit gets returned to your hand, then its Might is treated as null—a value that cannot be figured out. So you can’t compute Baited Hook’s ability successfully, because null + 1 is null, and no unit has null as a Might. You’ll reveal the top 5 cards of your Main Deck, but you won’t get to play any of them.

Layers

Layers! Everyone’s favorite topic. In addition to numbering these, as previously mentioned, we have done something rather radical to them. Our layers loop now! Layers in Riftbound apply repeatedly until each effect has been applied (or removed) once and layers have been evaluated with no objects changing. Loopy Layers! This helps Fiora actually work without being a paradox. Notably, we are keeping an eye on this. 

  • NEW RULE: Layers apply repeatedly until all applicable effects are applied or disqualified a single time and no objects have changed during one sequence of application.
  • CLARIFIED: Dependencies have been more clearly defined.
  • CLARIFIED: Method of resolving dependencies have been more clearly defined.
    • These are vanishingly rare, but forearmed is forewarned.

Triggered Ability Updates

  • CLARIFIED: Made clear how to identify triggered abilities, including “Nth time” abilities.
    • Notably, the terms that identify triggered abilities don’t have to appear at the start of the ability’s sentence. Sona. 
  • CLARIFIED: In the case of “Nth time” triggers, when the triggering event occurs at the specified N but more than one qualifying event occurs simultaneously, the “Nth Time” trigger will only trigger once.
  • CLARIFIED: Triggered abilities evaluate conditions from the destination of their object.
    • See our [FAQ] for more information on this—specifically the entries for Immortal Phoenix and Viktor, Leader.
  • NEW RULE: Several common trigger shapes have been defined: Play, Conquer, Hold, Attack, and Defend abilities.
  • NEW RULE: Attack and Defend triggers can happen once per combat, specifically the first time something gains the attacker or defender designation during that combat.
    • Note that this is a CHANGE from the FAQ as we further tested and iterated on the rules!

We had feedback from the community that our triggered abilities were sometimes hard to identify, so the rules now help with that. And by grouping things like “play effects” and “conquer effects,” we make it easier for rules and cards to refer to them and for players to understand what we mean (and don’t mean) when they do.

We also had some work that came out of the recent [FAQ]. We knew we wanted Attack and Defend triggers to be able to trigger even if a unit joined combat “late.” When we wrote the FAQ, we expected the rules update to allow those those triggers to potentially go off multiple times. After all, to quote our past selves, “moving a unit at Action speed isn’t easy to do, and doing it twice is even harder.” Since then, though, we decided that triggering Attack and Defend triggers multiple times didn’t feel right, and moving units repeatedly in and out of combat wasn’t something we wanted to reward. (We won’t stop you, though.)

Delayed Abilities

  • NEW RULE: Defined the concept of a delayed ability and how to identify them. 
  • NEW RULE: Any type of ability can be delayed. Added rules to clarify how those operate with delay.

A tool that was undefined but utilized can now be easily identified and understood.

Costs

  • CLARIFIED: Made clear that replaced costs are still paid costs.

Scoring

  • CLARIFIED: Conquering on defense has been clarified through the concept of contested status.

Burn Out

  • CLARIFIED: Made the conditions to Burn Out more clear.
  • CLARIFIED: Made the conditions to repeatedly Burn Out more clear.

Added more language to make clear the intention for Burn Out and when players should be triggering the situation. Also added examples and logistics to make clear when and how, specifically, players would hypothetically infinitely Burn Out. 

Add

  • CLARIFIED: ‘Add’ abilities finalize immediately like Units and Gear.
  • CLARIFIED: Focus and Priority do not pass on resolution of Add abilities.

Kill

  • CLARIFIED: Kill effect definition clarified.
  • CLARIFIED: Kill attribution rules clarified.

Hide/Hidden

  • CLARIFIED: Cards in the Champion Zone can now use their Hidden abilities.
  • CLARIFIED: Hidden costs [A], not [C].
  • CLARIFIED: Hidden’s targeting restrictions have been rearticulated as part of the broader targeting changes. 
  • CLARIFIED: Hidden cards gain Reaction when played from facedown—they aren’t just played as though they have it.

Hidden is one of our most complex mechanics. It allows you to hide, which is a specific action, but Hidden itself is a keyword, not an action. That is neither here nor there for this update, though, as the things most worth mentioning are related to things that occur after the card is facedown.

Of particular focus, hidden cards now gain Reaction, and the restrictions on targeting for cards played from facedown have been altered. The former is a minor change, and will not have a tangible impact on most players, but as outlined in the FAQ, the latter has a material impact to the way Zhonya’s Hourglass plays. This targeting change and change to hidden means that the card no longer restricts its replacement effect to the battlefield it was hidden at.

More details about the change are in the complete CR. This marks us trying to zero in on making Hidden play intuitively, and we anticipate authoring content in the future that leans in to the intuition as opposed to requiring players to know every gotcha and pitfall. 

Legion

  • CLARIFIED: Made clear the specific differences in Legion as a spell ability, play effect, and activated ability.

Accelerate

  • CLARIFIED: The cost of the ability always matches the domain of the unit that has the ability.
  • CLARIFIED: If the ability is ever on a unit with no domain or more than one domain, it becomes [A].

Recall

  • CLARIFIED: Recalls are only to the object’s base.
  • CLARIFIED: Recalls do not affect the state of the object.
  • CLARIFIED: Recalls are not moves.
